planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in a warm, sheltered, sunny site; Vranja is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer, but a sun trap is important since fruit needs a long, warm season to ripen fully.

directions: Vranja is a Balkan quince selection that became one of the most widely planted cultivars in British and northern European gardens for its large, downy, pear-shaped fruit and unusually showy spring bloom of pale pink flowers up to two inches across. The species is native to mountain slopes and tolerates real winter cold, but flowers open early enough to need a sheltered, sun-baked spot so fruit has a long enough warm season to swell and perfume the air before frost. Trees are self-fertile and productive without a second cultivar nearby, though yields are typically moderate rather than heavy. Harvest in mid-autumn once fruit turns deep golden-yellow and releases its strong floral aroma, then store briefly before cooking into jelly, paste, or preserves, since the raw flesh stays hard and astringent.

common_name: Rea's Mammoth Quince (Giant-Fruited American Heirloom Quince)

planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Rea's Mammoth is self-fertile and does not require a second quince cultivar for fruit set.

directions: Rea's Mammoth is a nineteenth-century sport of Orange Quince selected in California for fruit that runs noticeably larger than typical quince, often exceeding a pound apiece, with bright yellow skin and firm, intensely fragrant flesh well suited to jelly, paste, and baking. The self-fertile tree crops reliably on a compact frame, making it a practical choice for small orchards or a single dooryard specimen where space for a second pollinizer tree is not available. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and prune lightly each winter to keep an open canopy that sheds humidity and reduces fire blight pressure. Pick in mid-to-late fall once fruit turns fully golden and gives off its characteristic heavy quince perfume, and expect the raw flesh to remain hard and tart until cooked.
sources: NW Fruit / Western Washington Fruit Research Foundation

planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Bereczki is self-fertile and reliably productive without a second quince cultivar.

directions: Bereczki is a nineteenth-century Hungarian quince named for pomologist Mate Bereczki and still ranked among that country's best cultivars for its heavy, dependable crops of large, pear-shaped fruit. The juicy, sweet-tart yellow flesh turns a distinctive reddish hue once cooked, making it a favorite for jelly, paste, and preserves where color as well as flavor matters. Trees grow into a somewhat larger, vigorous framework than many quince selections, so give it a bit more room and prune in winter to maintain an open, airy canopy that discourages fire blight. Harvest in late September as fruit turns deep gold and fragrant; picked fruit stores in a cool space for several weeks before it needs to be cooked down.

planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Grand Traverse needs a compatible pollenizer such as an American hazelnut seedling or 'The Beast' nearby, since it will not set a crop alone.

directions: Grand Traverse was selected in Michigan by breeder Cecil Farris from a cross tracing back to Turkish tree hazel, giving it exceptional cold hardiness and good tolerance of eastern filbert blight compared with pure European filbert cultivars. Nuts are thin-shelled, fiber-free, and well flavored, borne on a vigorous tree that handles harsh continental winters better than Pacific Northwest hazelnut selections. Because it carries mixed parentage, plant it alongside an unrelated pollenizer such as a wild American hazelnut for reliable nut set, and space trees generously to accommodate its eventual tree-like habit. Harvest in early autumn as husks dry and nuts drop free; gather promptly from the ground to stay ahead of squirrels.

planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; plant a second chestnut cultivar such as 'Marigoule' or 'Bouche de Betizac' nearby for pollination, since chestnuts are largely self-incompatible.

directions: Precoce Migoule is a vigorous French hybrid between European and Japanese chestnut, discovered at an orchard near Brive-la-Gaillarde and prized for ripening its medium-to-large, glossy nuts up to two weeks ahead of Colossal and other later hybrids. That early harvest lets growers in shorter-season regions get a crop in before fall frost damages burs still on the tree, and the tree is also a heavy, well-timed pollen source for other sativa-type cultivars. Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun with a compatible cultivar nearby for cross-pollination, since a single chestnut tree will not produce nuts. Harvest in early-to-mid fall as spiny burs split open and nuts drop free.

planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Campbell CW3 sheds pollen early and benefits from a second heartnut seedling or cultivar with overlapping female bloom for best nut set.

directions: Campbell CW3 was selected by Ontario nut breeder Doug Campbell from superior heartnut seedlings and remains a parent behind several later Grimo Nut Nursery introductions, valued for staying more compact than seedling heartnut trees while still producing good crops of heart-shaped nuts. Kernels typically crack out in halves or whole pieces with a mild, sweet flavor much less oily than black walnut. Because it produces pollen early relative to when its own flowers are receptive, planting a second heartnut selection nearby improves fruit set even though some self-pollination can occur. Grow in deep, well-drained soil in full sun and harvest in early autumn once the husks soften and nuts drop free of the hull.
